name: Lion diet

lead: The lion diet allows only ruminant meat such as beef, plus salt and water. Followers cite leaner bodies and clearer skin, and it is a stricter version of the carnivore diet.

With food choice this narrow, calorie intake tends to fall, which is the route to a leaner look. Proponents describe it as removing all plant foods and other potential triggers, which they link to clearer skin. It spread through social media after public figures said they followed it, and no clinical trials of the lion diet itself have been found.

paras: People eat beef (and other ruminant meat), salt their food and drink water, often as an elimination-style stretch of weeks or months before reintroducing foods.

Dietetic bodies such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia call the carnivore diet a fad and cite raised LDL cholesterol, low fibre and vitamin deficiencies from excluding plant foods.

angle.text: Followers eat only ruminant meat, salt and water, aiming for lower calorie intake, a leaner body and clearer skin through a very restricted food list. No trials exist on the lion diet itself.

lead: The lion diet is a restrictive elimination diet consisting only of ruminant meat (typically beef), salt and water. It is the strictest form of the carnivore diet, which allows animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs.[1] People follow it with appearance goals in mind: losing body fat, reducing facial puffiness and calming skin, which adherents attribute to removing plant foods, dairy and processed ingredients that they suspect trigger inflammation.

It gained wider attention after Mikhaila Peterson, who began a carnivore diet in 2018 and went on to write and speak about the lion diet, and her father Jordan Peterson said they followed it, and it later became a viral TikTok trend.[1][2] A 2026 analysis of one month of Instagram content from 19 carnivore creators (1,169 posts) found a notable focus on health and disease statements, a strong emphasis on red meat, otherwise varied food recommendations, and a generally positive portrayal of the diet.[3]

Dietetic organisations such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia have called the carnivore diet a fad, and commentators raise nutrient-gap concerns.[1] A 2026 scoping review identified nine human studies of carnivore-style eating, which reported weight reduction and greater satiety in some participants alongside risks of nutrient shortfalls and raised LDL cholesterol; the review described the evidence as limited by small samples, short durations and lack of control groups.[4] No clinical trials of the lion diet itself have been found.

paras: The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, excludes fruits, vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and followers eat beef, pork, poultry and seafood, with some also eating dairy and eggs.[1] The lion diet narrows it further to ruminant meat, salt and water. Paul Saladino's 2024 animal-based diet is a looser variant that permits fruit, honey and raw dairy.[1]

Adherents often frame the lion diet as a short-term elimination protocol: the person removes everything but one food group, then reintroduces other foods one at a time to see which ones, if any, they react to.[1][2] Because the diet contains no fruit, vegetables, grains or dairy, it is also very low in carbohydrate and fibre. The 2026 scoping review defines the carnivore diet as an almost exclusively animal-based dietary pattern and notes that no standardised definition exists.[4]
Wikipedia distinguishes the carnivore diet from Inuit cuisine, which it says includes organs, plentiful seafood and raw meat, and historically included gathered plant foods.[1]

Exclusively animal diets have earlier precedents. Bernard Moncriff published a book on one in 1856 and spent a year eating only beef and milk, the Italian physician Arnaldo Cantani prescribed animal-based diets to diabetic patients in the 1870s, and in the 1880s James H. Salisbury promoted lean beef and hot water, which became known as the Salisbury diet.[1]

subs.h: The Petersons and the lion diet
paras: According to Wikipedia, Mikhaila Peterson (born 1992) was diagnosed with arthritis at age two, had joint replacements as a teenager, and also has celiac disease. In 2018 she began a carnivore diet, captioning an Instagram post with the line 'Beef, salt, water and bourbon = cured.' She started a blog, Don't Eat That, that discusses the lion diet as the most restrictive carnivore variant, and says her health improved on a meat-only intake.[2] Her health information is hosted on liondiet.com, and the Guardian reported that she briefly offered private consultations.[2]

Wikipedia's carnivore diet article says Jordan Peterson and Mikhaila Peterson were vocal adherents of the version consisting of only beef, salt and water, and that the lion diet became a viral TikTok fad.[1] Mikhaila Peterson has since built a podcast and YouTube channel with a large following, appeared on The Joe Rogan Experience and Piers Morgan Uncensored, and, per Wikipedia, planned a supplement brand; her blog drew criticism after the Rogan appearance from writers who accused it of promoting quackery.[2]

Shawn Baker, a former orthopaedic surgeon, promoted the broader carnivore diet on social media in 2018 and wrote a book on it.[1] In 2024 Paul Saladino popularised an animal-based variant adding fruit, honey and raw dairy to red meat.[1] The article also describes a strand of 'carnivore traditionalism' that favours grass-fed beef from small regenerative farms over industrial production.[1]

The 2026 Instagram analysis reported that the 19 creators studied (aged 25 to 64, with an average of about 157,758 followers) posted mainly health-related and disease-related statements, with ideology-related and politically relevant themes alongside.[3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: Strength-training forums such as T Nation host discussion of carnivore eating, including debate over whether dairy and eggs belong in it and whether eating like predators is a sensible model.[5][6] One poster wrote that they never understood carnivore dieters eating large amounts of cheese and butter, which lions do not;[5] another said lions do not eat eggs or milk;[6] a third argued that only humans eat a 'well balanced diet'.[7] Posters in another thread joke about imagining a training programme for people strictly on the diet, with broad jumps, sprints and shadow boxing.[8] A separate T Nation member posted a self-designed all-meat 'Predator Program' combining a gorging day, two fasting days and hard training, and asked for feedback.[9]

In looks-focused communities, interest centres on three expected effects: lower body fat because of high satiety and low calorie variety, less facial puffiness that followers attribute to removing processed foods and dairy, and clearer skin from an elimination approach. These are adherents' accounts; the research below does not measure facial or skin outcomes.

Wikipedia reports that the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia dismiss the carnivore diet as a fad, that nutrition scientists have warned it may be dangerous, and that the neurologist Steven Novella, writing in April 2023, called it the latest fad diet and described it as pseudoscientific, noting its high cost.[1] The article lists low fibre and constipation, raised LDL cholesterol, micronutrient shortfalls, links between high red meat intake and colon cancer and gout, and possible strain on the kidneys from very high protein intake.[1]

The scoping review lists potential shortfalls in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre. Its authors concluded that the diet may offer short-term benefits but carries substantial risks of nutrient deficiencies, and noted that one study described a deterioration in health.[4] Critics also point to the greenhouse-gas emissions of large-scale livestock farming.[1]
No studies found of the lion diet itself.

A 2026 scoping review in Nutrients searched PubMed, LIVIVO, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library and included nine human studies of the carnivore diet. Individual studies reported weight reduction, increased satiety and potential improvements in inflammatory or metabolic markers, while also identifying possible deficiencies in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre, elevated LDL and total cholesterol, and one case of deterioration in health. The authors described the quality of evidence as very limited because of small samples, short durations and no control groups.[4]
A one-month Instagram content analysis of 19 carnivore creators is a study of social media portrayals rather than of health outcomes in dieters.[3]

Followers describe leaner bodies, less water retention in the face and calmer skin on the diet. No controlled measurement of skin condition, facial swelling or body composition on a beef-only diet has been reported. The scoping review reports weight reduction and greater satiety in some participants of carnivore-style studies, which is the main body-composition finding in the literature.[4]

Related eating patterns include the broader carnivore diet, Saladino's animal-based diet, the historical Salisbury diet, ketogenic and low-carbohydrate diets, and conventional elimination diets in which foods are removed and reintroduced one at a time.[1]

lore.intro: The lion diet is discussed in forums as a stricter, more 'pure' version of carnivore eating, with debate over what counts as carnivore.

claims.claim: Eating only beef, salt and water eliminates the foods that make skin and face look inflamed.
People should eat like predators, so dairy and eggs are not really carnivore.
A meat-only diet is nutritionally complete.
A meat-only elimination diet can settle autoimmune and inflammatory problems.
Beef-only eating leads to leanness through satiety.
Social-media carnivore content shows the diet is healthy.

timeline.event: Bernard Moncriff publishes a book on an exclusively animal diet.[1]
Arnaldo Cantani prescribes animal-based diets to diabetic patients.[1]
James H. Salisbury promotes a lean beef and hot water diet.[1]
Shawn Baker promotes the carnivore diet online; Mikhaila Peterson begins a carnivore diet and starts a blog on the lion diet, and Jordan Peterson also follows it.[1][2]
The Guardian and other outlets cover Mikhaila Peterson's diet; her blog is criticised after her Joe Rogan appearance.[2]
Mikhaila Peterson's YouTube podcast channel begins.[2]
Neurologist Steven Novella calls the carnivore diet a pseudoscientific fad.[1]
Paul Saladino popularises a looser animal-based diet.[1]
